description: I’m interested in technology, science, and creative solutions to real-world problems. I love brainstorming, collaborating with people from different backgrounds, and turning ambitious ideas into working prototypes. I’m excited about NASA Space Apps and the opportunity to use data and technology to tackle global challenges. I’m looking for curious teammates with skills in AI/ML, Python, data science, web development.
summary:
On a long mission, astronauts can’t wait for a doctor on Earth to notice that something is wrong. Radiation, isolation, microgravity and life in a closed cabin slowly change the body and mind, and the crew often has to catch those changes themselves. We built ORBIT to help them do that.

ORBIT is a health-monitoring app that works fully offline. Short animated guides walk crew members through taking their own vitals, from blood pressure and ECG to lung function and eye checks. They can also log sleep, mood, workouts, skin checks and radiation dose.

ORBIT then helps make sense of it all. It compares each reading with that person’s normal range and charts trends over weeks. It flags readings that stay out of range and shows who on the crew needs attention first. When something looks off, crew can turn to a guided assessment, an evidence library built from NASA research, or a voice assistant that runs on board and never saves anything without a person’s approval.

Far from Earth, every minute of communication delay matters. ORBIT puts the tools for spotting and responding to health changes in the crew’s own hands.
details:
ORBIT is a health monitoring app for astronauts on long missions. It runs on a laptop or over the ship’s local network, and it doesn’t need internet to work, which was important to us since deep space missions won’t have a reliable connection to Earth.

The app is built around three things an astronaut needs to do: collect their health data, understand it, and figure out what to do about it.

For collecting data, we made short animated guides that show how to take each measurement, like heart rate, blood pressure, ECG, lung function, temperature and eye checks. You can also log sleep, mood, workouts, skin checks, wounds and radiation dose. All of it gets saved to that crew member’s health record.

To help make sense of the readings, ORBIT checks each one against that person’s normal range and labels it as normal, caution or critical. It also compares the past week to the past three weeks, so slow changes like a gradual rise in blood pressure are easier to spot. We didn’t want one bad reading to set off an alarm, so alerts only show up when something stays out of range for several checks in a row. There’s a crew status page that lists whoever needs attention first.

When something does look off, crew members can go through a guided health assessment or search our evidence library. We built the library from NASA research and organized it by the risks in the challenge: radiation, isolation, altered gravity, the closed cabin and immune changes. Every entry lists its sources. There’s also a 3D anatomy lab where you can drop a pin on the exact spot where something hurts and add notes to it.

The voice assistant is probably the feature we’re proudest of. It runs completely offline on the computer itself. You can ask it for someone’s latest readings, tell it to open a form and read out the values, or ask it to show the left knee on the 3D model. It answers questions using the evidence library and tells you where the information came from. It’s not allowed to save anything by itself, so a person always has to press Save or say “confirm save.” We also added an emergency check. If someone mentions bleeding, choking, chest pain or a crewmate passing out, the assistant reads first-aid steps we wrote ahead of time before the AI says anything else, and tells the crew to get the medical officer.

We built the main site with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and the voice assistant and anatomy tools with React and TypeScript. The server is in Python using FastAPI. For the voice side we used Pipecat to connect Silero (detects when you’re talking), Whisper (speech to text), the Qwen3 model through Ollama (writes the answers) and Kokoro (text to speech). The 3D body uses three.js and models from Z-Anatomy, and the charts use Recharts. We also included two optional online features, an ElevenLabs voice assistant and a photo check using Google Gemini, but you can switch them off with one toggle.

A few things we kept in mind the whole time: the app shouldn’t act like a doctor, so it never diagnoses anything. Stress and fatigue scores are private and never used to rank people. Astronauts might be tired, stressed or wearing gloves when they use it, so we tried to make it work by voice and keep the main screens simple.

We also added profiles of Mercury astronauts Scott Carpenter and Gordon Cooper using real NASA flight data. We thought it was a cool way to show the app working with real astronaut numbers, not just made-up test data.
